newsitem.title: FRANCE: Australia patches up nuclear row with France.
newsitem.headline: Australia patches up nuclear row with France.

text.p: Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer began mending fences in Paris on Monday with a call for more trade and an end to the bitter row over French nuclear tests in the South Pacific
Downer made it clear that it was back to business as usual after the dispute which had led to mutual threats of economic boycott. France ended the tests eight months ago.

"One of the purposes of my visit is to re-invigorate the Australia-France relationship and restore the momentum it had prior to the period of nuclear testing," Downer, the most senior Australian representative to visit Paris since the tests, told a lunch of the Australian Business in Europe (ABIE) group.
He expected to meet Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette later on Monday.

At the height of the row, Australia's then prime minister Paul Keating branded as "an act of stupidity" tests ordered by President Jacques Chirac to upgrade France's nuclear arsenal before abolishing testing forever.
Australia accused France of acting as a colonial power in the South Pacific, while Paris said Australia was seizing on the tests to try and drive France out of the region.

"Australia welcomes, and indeed encourages, France increasing its links with the Asia-Pacific region," Downer said. "It is important that our two countries work together to ensure the continued stability and economic development of the region."
France carried out its last test in January and said it was closing down its nuclear test range in French Polynesia.
It has since signed the Treaty of Rarotonga, making the South Pacific a nuclear-free zone, and announced it would sign a U.N. treaty outlawing all nuclear testing on September 24.
A conservative government took over in Australia last March from Labour, which had led the protests against the tests.
Downer said Australians had been "understandably upset", but a long-standing bilateral relationship could weather such rows.
"French investors are welcome in Australia...There are great opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region for countries such as France," he said.
French officials have described relations as convalescent and said they expected the visit to seal reconciliation.
Trade and investment were apparently unscathed despite some calls for boycott. Overall French exports to Australia rose in the test period, but some high-profile goods like wine suffered.
Most Australian exports to France, like uranium, coal and wool, are sold on long-term contracts and were unaffected.

Signalling a drive to boost Australian exports to France, Downer said trade was running very much in France's favour. "Australia therefore naturally wants to do more and expand the range of Australian products and services to France," he said.
French exports to Australia totalled 6.4 billion francs ($1.3 billion) in 1995, well above imports worth 4.4 billion francs.

French investments in Australia rose to a record total of 14 billion francs during the testing period, bolstered by French insurer Axa SA buying a 51 percent stake in Australian insurance group National Mutual Holdings last year for four billion francs.
Over the past decade, the number of French companies investing in Australia has doubled to about 200.
Downer is due to travel on to Berlin on Tuesday. He will also visit Britain, and the United Nations in New York.
